books.section: Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, D. Regional Specialization
Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, B. Advances in Technology
The North and the Textile Industry

stimulus.text: A print of Lowell, Massachusetts, made between 1840 and 1860, looks across the Merrimack River toward a long row of large brick mill buildings standing side by side along the water. Smaller houses stand nearby, and the river runs in the foreground. Lowell was built as a factory town, and its mills turned Southern cotton into cloth.
stimulus.source_note: View of Lowell, Massachusetts, 1840-1860, Library of Congress (LCCN94515606), via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The mills in the print stand along the Merrimack River mainly because

options.text: the river carried raw cotton up from the South
options.misconception: Cotton reached Lowell by ship and wagon, not up the Merrimack; the river's job was power, not transport.

options.text: falling water powered the mill machinery
federal law required textile mills to be built on rivers
options.misconception: No federal law placed mills on rivers; owners chose river sites for the power the water gave.

options.text: the river kept the mill buildings cool in summer
options.misconception: Cooling was not the point. The river turned waterwheels that drove the looms and spindles.

rationales.A: Cotton came to Lowell from Southern ports by sea and road. The Merrimack's value to the mills was its falling water.
rationales.B: Early factories ran on water power. Lowell was built where the Merrimack's falls could turn the wheels that drove the machinery.
rationales.C: Mill owners picked river sites freely. The government did not order factories onto rivers.
rationales.D: The buildings needed power far more than cool air. Waterwheels, not breezes, ran the looms.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the print. The mills crowd the riverbank, and the river runs fast in the foreground.
2. Ask what a river gave a factory in 1820. Before steam spread, falling water was the power source.
3. Put it together. Lowell sits on the Merrimack because its water turned the mill wheels.
Background: Steam power only began replacing waterwheels in factories in the years before the Civil War.
Remember: for an early factory, place follows power; find the power source first.
